items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The late Dizzy Gillespie and I, we were great friends for about 45, 50 years

ctx.x: How did he get his musical interest? Where did that come from? Seems he would be so occupied with making a living on the farm, that….did he work professionally?

He was a coal miner. And everyone there was a coal miner. And he used to listen to records. I think Bessie Smith was the most popular one there. And Mamie Smith. And I got interested in one that Louis Armstrong made with Bessie Smith. He made quite a few I think, him and Earl Hines and Coleman Hawkins. And that attracted my attention, and I began to listen to Louis Armstrong and from then on after I heard him play on these records I had no doubt in my mind I was going to try and be a trumpet player. I still am.…

items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Dizzy and all of us used to do that every morning. Charlie Shavers. We’d go someplace every morning, and play.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Dizzy and I got in a little -- we started playing some "Body and Soul" in a place in Philadelphia one night

ctx.x: Well, had you given him any trouble or --

No. Well, Charlie and Rama had played with Dizzy so they wanted somebody in the band that they had played with. You know, they were good buddies. And I'm from St. Louis, you know. But Dizzy and I got in a little -- we started playing some "Body and Soul" in a place in Philadelphia one night and I kind of made a little noise that night, playing "Body and Soul." So Lucky hired me back. And Dizzy went with Teddy Hill. Come the side 3 - end

But after we went from Philadelphia back to New York, that's when Bobby Moore took ill and I -- Herschel and Jo, they recommended me to Basie and I took his place, you know. And -- oh, that was the latter part of 1937. But I still wanted to learn more about music because when I joined Basie's band, it was nothing but head arrangements. Everything was head arrangements. They didn't have -- I bet they didn't have 10 manuscripts, you know.
